The Himalayan snowcock (Tetraogallus himalayensis) is a large-bodied phasianid occupying high-altitude scree slopes of the central Himalaya. Eggs are incubated for approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] at a consistent nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns with the extended incubation periods observed in other high-elevation galliforms. Upon hatching, chicks weigh roughly 47.9 grams [Wwb = roughly 47.9 grams], a value reflecting the substantial yolk reserves characteristic of precocial neonates. This initial mass is notably low compared to the ultimate wet weight achieved by adults, which reach around 2326 grams [Wwi = around 2326 grams] in females, though males typically attain a higher final mass of 2529 grams [Wwi = 2529 grams]. Field records indicate that females deposit a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], containing 8 to 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 8 to 12 eggs per clutch]; this relatively modest annual output likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the harsh alpine environment and the prolonged developmental requirements of the chicks.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], fledging occurs remarkably early, just 3 days after hatching [tx = 3 days after hatching]. This rapid achievement of flight capability is an adaptation to the steep, unstable terrain of the species' habitat, allowing nestlings to escape predators and follow their parents across treacherous slopes almost immediately. The timing of fledging is closely tied to the pace of feather development, which is accelerated in these cold, high-altitude environments where the risk of hypothermia is elevated. Following this initial independence, juvenile birds enter a period of sustained somatic growth, during which they must accumulate sufficient body reserves to survive the severe winter conditions. The brevity of the fledging interval is unusual among galliforms of comparable body size and underscores the selective pressures operating in the extreme alpine zone where the Himalayan snowcock resides. Chicks that fail to achieve flight within this narrow window are considerably more vulnerable to predation and environmental stress.

The progression to sexual maturity follows a slower trajectory compared to the rapid onset of locomotor independence. Puberty is reached at 100 days after hatching [tp = 100 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a timing that corresponds to the near-completion of skeletal growth and the attainment of a body mass approaching adult dimensions. Gonadal recrudescence is delayed until the bird has achieved sufficient fat reserves, which is critical for sustaining the energetic demands of courtship, territory defense, and subsequent reproductive activity. This age at maturity is typical for a species of this body mass within the Phasianidae, where the trade-off between continued somatic investment and the initiation of reproductive effort is finely balanced. The high metabolic costs of thermoregulation at elevation, coupled with the short growing season, likely push the onset of puberty toward this later date, ensuring that only well-conditioned individuals enter the breeding population.

First reproduction in the Himalayan snowcock occurs at 1 year after hatching [tR = 1 year after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], representing a full annual cycle from the individual's own emergence. This interval implies that birds hatched in late spring become reproductively active the following spring, when snowmelt exposes the nesting substrate and initiates the flush of alpine vegetation that supports their insectivorous prey. The delay between pubertal maturation at 100 days and actual breeding at 365 days is likely due to the need to acquire a high-quality territory and a mate, as well as the necessity of completing the energetically demanding molt into definitive adult plumage. Some individuals may defer breeding further if conditions are unfavorable, but the species' life-history strategy generally favors early reproduction to maximize lifetime output given the relatively short window of favorable conditions each year. The annual reproductive schedule is tightly synchronized with the brief alpine growing season.

Longevity in this species is moderate for a galliform of its size, with the maximum lifespan estimated at 5.2 years [am = 5.2 years] under the thermal conditions of active metabolism at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Field observations suggest that few individuals survive beyond four or five breeding seasons, with mortality concentrated during the harsh winter months when food availability declines and thermoregulatory costs peak. The wet weight of the egg at the start of incubation was 77.3 grams [Ww0 = 77.3 grams], representing the initial maternal investment in each offspring; this mass is substantially higher than the mass at hatching due to the absorption of egg-derived water and the initiation of feeding. The relatively short lifespan reflects the combined pressures of predation, severe weather, and the energetic demands of reproduction in an extreme environment, favoring a life-history strategy that prioritizes early and efficient breeding over extended somatic maintenance. This species thus exemplifies the trade-offs inherent in high-altitude avian life histories.
